red.focus: Research the evidence supporting a causal claim
red.summary: A legal narrative should not turn a sequence of events into an unsupported causal accusation. Learn to find facts that support or challenge a claimed connection.
checklist: I can differentiate chronology from causation
I can list plausible alternative causes
I can record the source of each factual assertion

sections.title: A Timeline Is a Beginning
sections.body_md: A client starts a new job and develops back pain a week later. The order of events does not prove the workplace caused the injury. Research must identify work tasks, medical records, prior symptoms and other possible explanations while respecting privacy. The governing claim may also define the required causal link differently from ordinary conversation. A legal researcher begins with a reliable timeline, then seeks evidence about mechanisms and alternative causes rather than treating the sequence as proof.

sections.title: Ask What Would Change the Answer
sections.body_md: Suppose an accident report says a safety device failed. Maintenance records, photographs and a manufacturer's technical information could help determine why. A good research note identifies what each source can show and where it is weak. The task is not to collect every possible document. It is to find information capable of distinguishing the main causal explanations. That approach produces shorter, more meaningful analysis and reduces the risk of overlooking a decisive fact.

sections.title: State the Link Honestly
sections.body_md: An inference may be plausible but not yet established under the law's proof standard. A lawyer should label hypotheses, disputed facts and verified records distinctly. Expert assistance may be needed for medicine, engineering or statistics, while the legal decision maker determines the consequences under applicable law. Clear writing explains why the evidence supports a causal proposition instead of relying on dramatic storytelling. Clients deserve accurate assessments because mistaken conclusions can affect health, compensation and freedom.

yellow.focus: Verify causal conclusions using distinct sources
yellow.summary: Learn to combine factual records, legal standards and expert evidence without confusing their functions. Identify which causal propositions remain uncertain and why.
checklist: I can trace a factual conclusion to records
I can distinguish expert opinion from a legal holding
I can identify a factual gap in a causation argument

sections.title: Records and Opinions Serve Different Roles
sections.body_md: A hospital record can establish treatment dates and recorded symptoms, but may not resolve what caused an illness. An expert opinion may interpret the records through medical knowledge. A court then evaluates the evidence under its legal standards. Research quality depends on keeping those roles separate. When a source states that exposure 'could' cause a condition, do not silently translate the statement into a conclusion that it did cause this person's condition.

sections.title: Follow the Logic of the Report
sections.body_md: An engineering expert may conclude a beam failed because of corrosion. The researcher should identify the inspection methods, measurements, alternative causes considered and assumptions. A strong explanation permits another reader to see how the conclusion follows from evidence. If the report merely repeats the client's account, it offers less independent support than its professional format suggests. The lawyer's duty is to assess relevance and reliability, not to accept every technical statement uncritically.

sections.title: Causation Has a Legal Side
sections.body_md: A factual connection does not necessarily determine the scope of compensable loss. Legal systems may impose separate requirements about remoteness, protected interests or foreseeability. Research must identify those tests from controlling sources. The final memo should state what evidence shows about events and what legal rule assigns responsibility for resulting harm. Keeping factual and normative questions distinct makes the advice clearer and more defensible.

orange.focus: Research statistics responsibly for causal claims
orange.summary: Advanced causal research requires separating association, confounding and individual attribution. Learn how method and sampling affect the weight of empirical evidence.
checklist: I can recognize confounders and selection bias
I can read a statistical finding without exaggeration
I can compare empirical conclusions with legal burdens

sections.title: Correlation Does Not Finish the Inquiry
sections.body_md: A study finds more illness among employees exposed to a substance, but those workers also differ in age or other exposures. A researcher should ask whether the study controlled for likely confounders and how participants were selected. Statistical association can be important evidence, yet it is not identical to establishing a mechanism or individual cause. Legal research must identify what a statistic actually estimates before using it in an argument about a person's liability.

sections.title: Precision Is Not Certainty
sections.body_md: A narrow confidence interval may indicate that a particular estimate is measured precisely within the study's model, but it cannot guarantee the model is unbiased. Missing data, misclassified exposure and selection effects may still matter. The lawyer should examine the assumptions and limitations reported by qualified experts. Describing a study as conclusive because its numerical presentation looks sophisticated can mislead a court and a client. Every quantitative statement needs a careful account of what was measured.

sections.title: Connect the Research to the Legal Question
sections.body_md: Different legal systems and causes of action require different proof thresholds and causal elements. A statistical finding may inform a regulatory risk assessment without establishing the causation necessary for private damages. The analysis must state which legal standard applies, what the evidence satisfies, and which uncertainties remain. A court may lawfully weigh expert evidence differently from a public health agency because the institutional task is different. Clear research explains rather than hides that distinction.

black.focus: Audit empirical legal research and attribution ethics
black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate the methodological and moral stakes of using probabilistic evidence to assign legal responsibility. Develop a research protocol that is both scientifically cautious and legally actionable.
checklist: I can critique causal methods under observational uncertainty
I can assess competing error costs in legal attribution
I can design evidence requests that reduce asymmetry

sections.title: The Model Is Not the World
sections.body_md: Causal estimates depend on assumptions about measurement, missing variables and the mechanisms connecting observed events. An advanced legal researcher should identify those assumptions explicitly, check whether they are testable, and explain how sensitive the conclusion is to alternatives. A persuasive numerical estimate without methodological transparency may create false certainty. This matters deeply when courts are asked to assign blame, impose penalties or award compensation for harms that science cannot trace to one source with precision.

sections.title: Uncertainty Is Distributed by Law
sections.body_md: A strict proof threshold can leave genuinely injured people without a remedy when evidence is held by the defendant or lost over time. A relaxed threshold can impose liability on a person who did not cause the harm. Legal presumptions and public compensation schemes sometimes address these problems under different rationales. A doctoral analysis should state which errors a proposal tolerates, what evidence exists and who can realistically obtain it. Fairness requires more than choosing the most sympathetic litigant.

sections.title: Evidence Governance Protects Everyone
sections.body_md: Research involving health records, employment data or environmental monitoring may reveal sensitive information about nonparties. A robust protocol specifies lawful access, minimization, technical reliability, review and retention. It should also include adverse hypothesis testing and disclosure of material methodological limits. The final legal opinion must separate empirical findings from normative judgments about responsibility. Great lawyering protects victims through rigorous investigation without treating the rights of other people as expendable.
